transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Honestly, in long meetings, people will talk directly to me and I just zone out—I realize afterward I didn’t really hear what they were saying. This has become a major issue over the last two years since a work restructuring put me in a leadership role with constant back-to-back meetings. It's incredibly embarrassing, and I'm worried it's starting to affect my career.

Before these work changes two years ago, did you have similar problems with attention or zoning out earlier in life, like in school or in other jobs? Or did this only start after the leadership role and increased stress began?

Looking back, these issues actually date back to my childhood; even in elementary school, my teachers wrote on report cards that I was always out of my seat, talking over classmates, and getting sent to the hallway because I couldn't sit still. I still did well on tests, so it wasn't a huge academic issue then, but these lifelong tendencies only became truly unmanageable recently with the intense demands of my new leadership role.
Do these attention or restlessness problems also affect you outside of work, like at home, in conversations, while driving, or when managing bills and daily tasks? Can you give one or two examples?

Yes, they definitely affect my life at home and my relationship. For example, if I try to sit and watch a movie with my partner for more than half an hour, I get this wired, crawling feeling inside and feel like I have to get up. I’m also constantly on the go reorganizing things instead of relaxing, which is starting to strain our relationship because I just can't sit and unwind with them.

Have there been times when your restlessness and nonstop activity came in clear episodes lasting several days where you needed much less sleep than usual and felt unusually energized or euphoric? Or have these attention and activity problems been pretty constant since childhood rather than coming in episodes?

No, I've never had sudden episodes of feeling euphoric or needing less sleep; these issues have been pretty constant for as long as I can remember. Even back in elementary school, my teachers would write on my report cards that I was always out of my seat, talking over classmates, and struggling to sit still or wait my turn. It has always been a continuous pattern rather than something that comes and goes in waves.

Besides work and home, have these attention or restlessness problems caused significant issues in any other settings, such as school, friendships, finances, driving, or daily responsibilities? What are the main problems they’ve caused there?

Currently, the issues are mostly concentrated at work and home, but looking back, school was definitely a major setting where these problems showed up. In elementary school, teachers frequently wrote on my report cards about me being out of my seat, talking over classmates, and being sent to the hallway because I couldn't sit still or wait my turn. Even though I was smart and got good grades, it was a constant struggle back then.
Do you also have problems with organization and follow-through, like missing deadlines, losing things, forgetting appointments, or leaving tasks unfinished? If so, which of these happens most often?

I don't really struggle with organizing, losing things, or missing deadlines, as I tend to be quite disciplined and competitive. My main issues are much more about staying focused during those long meetings and managing my constant restlessness.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a lifelong, non-episodic pattern beginning in childhood with prominent hyperactivity/impulsivity (out of seat, talking over others, unable to sit still, difficulty waiting turn) and ongoing adult restlessness plus inattentive zoning out. Symptoms are present across multiple settings (school, work, home) and now cause clear occupational and relationship impairment. Bipolar episodic symptoms were denied, and the presentation is most consistent with ADHD, disturbance of activity and attention.
